en: Into the infidels' land
You lead the Muslims.
Of such a multitude of people,
My Jakyp, you will become the pillar!
The Creator has undone your calamities;
Rich Jakyp,
No unfulfilled longing is left to you.
A lion will be born of you,
With all twelve parts of his body sound.
The youngest of six lions,
God's truly beloved servant,
Illustrious, great in name,
Both a champion and a lion,
A sovereign hero of surpassing fortune,
Such a son you are going to have.”
The Muslims, with Akbaltay at their head,
The Muslims raised their hands,
And gave their blessing with raised voices.
Jakyp's wife Chyyyrdy,
She too came out weeping aloud:
“Day after day, until this day,
There is no child to give us hope.
Let us put aside all sorrow;
Of these countless, useless herds,
Let us slaughter all the horses.
Let us scatter our possessions,
Open the mouths of our chests;
The great herds we have gathered,
Let us give them all away.
In this deceitful world,
Let us spend this faithless wealth
And ask the world for a little camel-calf!”
As though stabbed in a tender gland,
The hero Jakyp sprang up:
“I will not squander my herds,
I will not let my strength drain away.
I cannot afford to scatter livestock,
Nor have you a child being born.
I will not devise things for what does not exist,
I will not feast for your nonexistent child,
I will not destroy livestock for nothing!
I will not follow empty words,
I will not make plans because I saw a dream.
Confounded woman, I will not hold a feast!”
As they began the undertaking,
Rich Jakyp quarreled with his senior wife.
“I have an omen for such a thing:
We may yet have a child.
My senior wife,
Abandon hope only after three years!
The head of the herd is the dun mare,
The head of the household is the barren wife.
The dun mare goes without a foal,
The barren wife has not given birth.
If my dun mare foals, she will bear a racing steed;
The dun mare's foal,
The strongest of foals,
When born will become a noble warhorse;
Whoever asks for it will become a stranger.
Ridden on scouting missions, it will not tire;
Ridden with the baggage train, it will not ail;
Ridden into combat, it will not falter;
Ridden six months, it will not grow lean.
Until it reaches sixty asyy,
Its teeth will not wear and it will not grow old,
It will not panic at a shout;
Even if a din splits the earth,
It will not set one foot wrong.
Its bearing lofty, its back straight,
My senior wife,
Abandon hope only after three years!
If my dun mare foals, she will bear a racing steed;
Such will be its looks and form.
My straps have a double girth:
Such is the omen I have made.
If the barren wife gives birth, she will bear a falcon.
Let us banish all sorrow;
If God gives us one son,
Let us give him the name the people have spoken.
He will gird his waist with a leather belt;
If the barren wife bears a son,
Though an army of seven tümen comes,
He will enter it alone and attack.
He will be a back to brace our strength;
If God grants a son,
He will be a lion beyond mortal men,”
Rich Jakyp spoke these words.
That dear, great rich man Jakyp
Had words without end;
He would not feast before seeing a child:
Such was his stinginess with livestock.
Akbaltay gave his blessing.
In the marshes of broad Altay,
As the Kyrgyz lay in sorrow,
Days lingered, nights passed,
Summer passed, autumn reached its middle.
In the season of fatness,
A full three months had passed.
The senior wife named Chyyyrdy,
That wife of Jakyp's,
Was pregnant and had cravings.
He slaughtered eighty mares from the herd;
She was not satisfied with their meat.
That senior wife Chyyyrdy
Did not cease her cravings at all.
A nine headed by a camel,
Again Jakyp slaughtered livestock.
Before his senior wife,
He placed the meat he had slaughtered.
She did not eat the slaughtered meat,
She did not call it food.
“Find me lion's meat,” she said;
The senior wife would not give in.
No hunter could be found to shoot a lion,
Nor any lion's meat obtained.
That senior wife Chyyyrdy,
“Oh, for lion's meat!” she said.
From her dear quail-like eyes,
Tears fell drop by drop;
She wept as never before.
From her dear currant-black eyes,
She wept in sorrow.
“If only I could see lion's meat,” she said,
“Then I could die,” she said.
Hunched over like a quail,
The senior wife crouched down;
Gathering tears in her eyes,
The senior wife poured them out.
Without sleep at night,
Thus the senior wife wept.
Without sleep by day,
“O God, lion's meat!” she said,
Sighing and gasping without cease.
The senior wife took to her bed,
Brought suffering upon their heads.
Where could lion's meat be found?
The senior wife made a great turmoil.
“If only I could find lion's meat,” she said,
“And put it in my cauldron,” she said,
“And eat my fill in earnest,” she said,
“And quench my craving,” she said,
“Then I could die,” she said,
“And behold Judgment Day,” she said.
So the senior wife prayed.
At that time rich Jakyp,
His great herds of all four kinds,
He spent in search of a lion.
No lion's meat could be found;
The forty Kyrgyz households all wept.
He opened up the bounty of his herds,
Had them search for lion's meat,
Sent them roaming through many cities.
Among the forty households,
Akbaltay was the capable one;
Akbaltay found a plan.
The forty Kyrgyz households gathered;
Ninety camel-loads of wheat
They collected as a levy.
Forty hunters from forty households
Set out to hunt a lion.
Setting forth on a hunting expedition,
Traveling far, sparing not themselves,
The hunters could find no lion;
They stood there bewildered.
With Baltay and Jakyp at their head,
Ninety camel-loads of wheat
They gave to Kochku.
He had shot a lion,
Kochku, the Chinese hunter.
The lion's meat was found;
The forty Kyrgyz households, the poor people,
Their honor was thereby preserved,
The thing they lacked was found.
All the Kyrgyz cried aloud,
Prepared an offering to Baabedin,
Made their vows to Baabedin.
Their calves pattering about,
They seized and slaughtered them;
Those with means slaughtered camels,
The prosperous slaughtered mares.
Quickly voicing each wish,
Devising a feast beyond imagining,
The forty Kyrgyz households, the poor people,
All joined together in feasting.
Akbaltay and your Jakyp said:
“My beloved people,
The lion's meat has been found.
If this child is born,
A child like a lion will be granted us!”
Rich Jakyp spoke these words:
“My livestock and my life,
Take them as your spoils, my people,” he said.
“Leave me two and take one,
Leave my mounts and take my camels,
Take my red-tailed elephants;
My precious people, heed my words.
I ask this of you, hear me!
White-bearded elders, listen;
Forty Kyrgyz households, listen, every one!
The Black Kalmyk and Manchu peoples,
We live in their midst.
‘Rich Jakyp's wife
Has a craving for lion's meat’:
To the Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
Let no whisper of this reach them.
The wife who has these cravings,
Lest they smash our stone fortress,
Slaughter this entire people,
And drag her away to Beijing.
Before she can bear, before she gives birth,
Let them not destroy us all together.
We Kyrgyz were a people under sentence;
There were many Kalmyks in Altay.
The news of this wife,
If the Kalmyks hear it, they will not leave us safe,
They will never let us prosper.
Can a person put their trust
In those called Manchu infidels?
If they hear, they will not let us prosper;
The wife who has these cravings,
If they seize her, they will not leave us safe.”
Rich Jakyp spoke these words:
“My people, keep your mouths shut,” he said.
“By telling the Kalmyks,
Do not dig my pit,
Do not boil my misery.”
Jakyp pleaded and said this;
Akbaltay rose with force:
“Enough, Jakyp, my hero;
What you have said is wise,” he said.
“To the Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
Whoever whispers a word,
His seven forefathers are infidels,” he said.
“The wife who craves lion's meat,
Whether she bears a boy or a girl,
Whatever it may be,
That she will bear a lion, a hero,
I learned from old traditions,
I asked those who know.
When this Chyyyrdy bears, she will bear a lion,
She will bear a fierce gray-maned hero.
For these Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
If you live, my people, you will see,
She will bear poison steeped and ready;
For us true Kyrgyz, she will bear a banner.
She will bear a back to brace our strength,
She will bear a lion to bind at our waist.
You were forty Kyrgyz households;
Chew white wheat flour as your pledge.
‘She craved lion's meat’:
My people, hold the Quran and swear not to tell!”
When they heard this, the Kyrgyz people
Swore an oath on pain of death,
Quickly gave their promise,
Promised with sobbing cries.
The Kyrgyz people, every one,
